title: IPO Report Card: 30 to 60 Days After Listing — September 2026
description: This report covers 40 companies that listed on the stock exchange between 31 and 59 days ago. 23 companies (about 57.5%) are currently trading above their ini.

faq.a: An IPO (Initial Public Offering) is when a private company first offers its shares to the public to raise money, allowing ordinary investors to buy a part of the company.

An SME IPO is an IPO by a Small and Medium Enterprise (SME). These are usually smaller companies that list on a separate platform of the stock exchange, like NSE Emerge or BSE SME, with different rules compared to mainboard IPOs.

faq.q: How do I apply for an IPO?
faq.a: You can apply for an IPO through your bank's ASBA (Applications Supported by Blocked Amount) facility or through your stockbroker's platform. The money is blocked in your account and only debited if you are allotted shares.

Share allotment is the process where shares are distributed to applicants after an IPO closes. If an IPO is oversubscribed, you might not get all the shares you applied for, or even any shares at all.

faq.q: What is a lot size in an IPO?
faq.a: A lot size is the minimum number of shares you must apply for in an IPO. You cannot apply for fewer shares than the lot size, and applications must be in multiples of the lot size.

corrections.note: Corrected the lock-in period details for anchor investors based on SEBI regulations and softened an unverifiable summary statistic by attributing it to the article's own data.

edits.why: The original claim of 23 companies trading above IPO price was a summary statistic based on the provided table, which is attributed to chittorgarh.com. Without direct access to the live data on chittorgarh.com for the specific date (September 2026) and the exact IPOs considered, it's impossible to independently verify this aggregate claim. The article itself states the data is from chittorgarh.com, which is a known source for IPO data. The corrected text softens the claim to what is supported by the article's own table and attributes the data to the source.

The specific duration of the lock-in period for anchor investors is not universally 'usually 30 days' and is better detailed in the subsequent correction. Removing the specific number here makes the statement more generally accurate.

The original claim reversed the lock-in percentages for anchor investors. SEBI regulations state that 50% of the shares allotted to anchor investors are locked in for 90 days, and the remaining 50% are locked in for 30 days from the date of allotment.

fact_check.summary: The article provides a generally accurate overview of IPOs and related concepts, with most factual claims aligning with SEBI regulations and common understanding of the IPO process in India. However, one specific claim regarding anchor investor lock-in periods is incorrect.
